a1-copula.title: The Noun-Class Copula: ву / ю / ду
a1-copula.pattern: [subject] + ву (masculine) / ю (feminine) / ду (default, abstract) -- negative: вац / яц / дац
a1-copula.explanation: Chechen's "to be" isn't one fixed word -- it changes shape to agree with the grammatical class of its subject. A male referent takes ву (Со дика ву -- Ӏ am well, said by a man), a female referent takes ю (Со дика ю -- said by a woman), and most other subjects -- abstract statements and categories -- take ду. Each has a matching negative: вац, яц, дац.
a1-copula.fact: This class-agreement system is one of the defining features of the Northeast Caucasian language family Chechen belongs to -- the same в-/й-/д- markers shown here on the copula reappear as prefixes on many other verbs and adjectives throughout the language, not just this one word. A fourth form, бу, exists for a further noun class (confirmed textbook examples: малх бу -- "there is sun/it's sunny", and Ӏаж бу -- "it's an apple") -- its full usage range isn't covered here yet, only these two specific attested words.

dialogue.native: Со хьан ваша ву. Со дика ву.
dialogue.en: I am your brother. I am well.

a1-pronouns.title: Personal Pronouns & Their Genitive (Possessive) Forms
a1-pronouns.pattern: со→сан (my) · хьо→хьан (your) · иза→цуьнан (his/her) · тхо→тхан (our, excl.) · вай→вайн (our, incl.) · шу→шун (your, pl.) · уьш→церан (their)
a1-pronouns.explanation: Chechen forms possessives by putting the personal pronoun into its genitive case, not with a separate possessive word: со (Ӏ) becomes сан (my), хьо (you) becomes хьан (your), иза (he/she/it) becomes цуьнан (his/her). Chechen also splits "we" in two: тхо/тхан excludes the listener, вай/вайн includes them.
a1-pronouns.fact: The noun "name" (цӀе) is grammatically feminine (й-class) no matter whose name is being given -- Сан цӀе Ахьмад ю ("My name is Ahmad") takes ю even though Ahmad himself would take ву -- the copula agrees with цӀе, the word for "name" itself, not with the person it names.

dialogue.native: Сан цӀе Ахьмад ю. Хьан цӀе хӀун ю?
dialogue.en: My name is Ahmad. What is your name?

a2-comparative.title: Comparative & Superlative
a2-comparative.explanation: The comparative adds -x (or -ax after a consonant) to an adjective: хаза (beautiful) → хазах (more beautiful). The noun being compared against takes its own suffix, -л/-l: сан машина хьан машинал хазах ю (my car is prettier than your car, literally "...than-your-car more-beautiful is"). The superlative simply places уггар ("the most") before the plain adjective, with no extra ending needed.
a2-comparative.fact: Chechen's comparative construction packs the entire English phrase "than your car" into a single suffixed word, машинал -- there's no separate word for "than" at all, the case ending on the compared noun does that job by itself.

dialogue.native: Хьан машина хьенан машинал хазах юй?
dialogue.en: Whose car is your car prettier than?

dialogue.native: Сан машина хьан машинал хазах ю.
dialogue.en: My car is prettier than your car.

a2-reflexive-possession.title: Reflexive vs. Non-Reflexive Possession: шен / цуьнан
a2-reflexive-possession.pattern: шен (his/her OWN) vs. цуьнан (his/her, someone else's)
a2-reflexive-possession.explanation: Chechen distinguishes two different "his/her": шен marks that the possessor and the subject of the sentence are the SAME person (a true reflexive), while цуьнан marks that they're different people. Цунна шен йиша йеза (he loves his OWN sister) versus цунна цуьнан йиша йеза (he loves his -- someone else's -- sister) differ only in this one word, but mean two different things entirely.
a2-reflexive-possession.fact: This is a real, meaningful ambiguity English simply doesn't mark -- "he loves his sister" is genuinely unclear in English about whether it's his own sister or another man's, while Chechen is forced to specify it every single time a 3rd-person possessive is used.

dialogue.native: Цунна шен йиша йезий, цуьнан йиша йезий?
dialogue.en: Does he love his own sister, or someone else's sister?

b1-dative-experiencer.title: Dative Experiencer ("Psych") Verbs
b1-dative-experiencer.explanation: Verbs describing emotion, liking, or perception put the person who experiences the feeling in the DATӀVE case, not the nominative/absolutive the way English "Ӏ like" does: суна лаьмнаш хазахета (Ӏ like mountains, literally "to-me mountains seem-beautiful"). The verb still agrees with the noun-class of the thing being liked, not with the experiencer.
b1-dative-experiencer.fact: The same verb деза is "labile": with a dative subject it means "to like/love" (суна ... деза), but with an ERGATӀVE subject plus an infinitive it shifts to mean "need to" (ас бепиг дан деза -- Ӏ need to make bread) -- one verb, two case-frames, two related-but-distinct meanings.

dialogue.native: Сан цӀе Ахьмад ю. Суна лаьмнаш хазахета.
dialogue.en: My name is Ahmad. I like mountains.

b1plus-yesno-particle.title: Yes/No Questions: -й/-и
b1plus-yesno-particle.explanation: Chechen yes/no questions add the particle -й (after a vowel-final verb, e.g. the copula) or -и (after a consonant) directly onto the tensed verb, along with a rise in tone: воьду (I go) becomes воьдий (do you/I go?), ву (is) becomes вуй (is he/she?). WH-questions never take this particle -- the WH-word alone is enough to mark the question.
b1plus-yesno-particle.fact: This single suffix is doing exactly the job that English does with word order alone ("you go" -> "do you go") -- Chechen keeps the same subject-verb order in both the statement and the question, and lets one small suffix carry the entire distinction.

dialogue.en: Do you go to work by bus?
No, I go to work by car.

b1plus-wh-quantity.title: WH-Questions of Quantity: маса & мел
b1plus-wh-quantity.explanation: Маса asks about a countable quantity: маса дешархо ву кху чохь? (how many students are in this room?). Мел asks about an uncountable amount: мел ахча ду дешархочуьнгахь? (how much money does the student have?). Both stay in place where the answer would go, like other Chechen WH-words, rather than moving to the front of the sentence.
b1plus-wh-quantity.fact: Chechen has a whole family of distinct WH-words for "how": муха (how, manner), маса (how many, count), мел (how much, amount), and масазза (how many times, frequency) -- English collapses several of these into one word, but Chechen keeps them grammatically separate.

dialogue.en: How many students are in this room?
In this room there are 10 students.
